questions.title: GATE CSE 2008 | Question: 1
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
$\displaystyle \lim_{x \to \infty}\frac{x-\sin x}{x+\cos x}$ equals

  1. $1$
  2. $-1$
  3. $\infty$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.

questions.title: GATE IT 2008 | Question: 2
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
A sample space has two events $A$ and $B$ such that probabilities $P(A\cap B) = \dfrac{1}{2}, P(A') = \dfrac{1}{3}, P(B') =\dfrac{1}{3}$. What is $P(A\cup B)$ ?

  1. $\left(\dfrac{11}{12}\right)$
  2. $\left(\dfrac{10}{12}\right)$
  3. $\left(\dfrac{9}{12}\right)$
  4. $\left(\dfrac{8}{12}\right)$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Complement probabilities and inclusion-exclusion give 5/6; keyed option matches.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2008 | Question: 2
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
If $P, Q, R$ are subsets of the universal set U, then $$(P\cap Q\cap R) \cup (P^c \cap Q \cap R) \cup Q^c \cup R^c$$ is

  1. $Q^c \cup R^c$
  2. $P \cup Q^c \cup R^c$
  3. $P^c \cup Q^c \cup R^c$
  4. U

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Factored the P/P-complement terms and applied De Morgan's law; keyed option matches.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2008 | Question: 3
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
The following system of equations

  • $x_1 + x_2 + 2x_3 = 1$
  • $x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 = 2$
  • $x_1 + 4x_2 + αx_3 = 4$

has a unique solution. The only possible value(s) for $α$ is/are

  1. $0$
  2. either $0$ or $1$
  3. one of $0, 1$, or $-1$
  4. any real number

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Determinant is alpha-5; no listed option states all alpha except 5, matching the MTA disposition.

questions.title: GATE IT 2008 | Question: 21
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following first order formulae is logically valid? Here $\alpha(x)$ is a first order formula with $x$ as a free variable, and $\beta$ is a first order formula with no free variable.

  1. $[\beta \rightarrow (\exists x, \alpha(x))] \rightarrow [\forall x, \beta \rightarrow \alpha(x)]$
  2. $[\exists x, \beta \rightarrow \alpha(x)] \rightarrow [\beta \rightarrow (\forall x, \alpha(x))]$
  3. $[(\exists x, \alpha(x)) \rightarrow \beta] \rightarrow [\forall x, \alpha(x) \rightarrow \beta]$
  4. $[(\forall x, \alpha(x)) \rightarrow \beta] \rightarrow [\forall x, \alpha(x) \rightarrow \beta]$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Truth-condition analysis confirms option C is valid; key matches.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2008 | Question: 21
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
The minimum number of equal length subintervals needed to approximate $\int_1^2 xe^x\,dx$ to an accuracy of at least $\frac{1}{3}\times10^{-6}$ using the trapezoidal rule is

  1. $1000e$
  2. $1000$
  3. $100e$
  4. $100$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Composite trapezoid bound gives n>=1000e; integer ceiling is 2719 and keyed threshold option matches.

questions.title: GATE IT 2008 | Question: 22
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following is the negation of $[∀ x, α → (∃y, β → (∀ u, ∃v, y))]$

  1. $[∃ x, α → (∀y, β → (∃u, ∀ v, y))]$
  2. $[∃ x, α → (∀y, β → (∃u, ∀ v, ¬y))]$
  3. $[∀ x, ¬α → (∃y, ¬β → (∀u, ∃ v, ¬y))]$
  4. $[∃ x, α \wedge (∀y, β \wedge (∃u, ∀ v, ¬y))]$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Negated each quantifier and implication in order; option D matches.

questions.title: GATE IT 2008 | Question: 23
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
What is the probability that in a randomly chosen group of $r$ people at least three people have the same birthday?

  1. $1-\dfrac{365-364 \dots (365-r+1)}{365^{r}}$
  2. $\dfrac{365 \cdot 364 \dots (365-r+1)}{365^r}+ ^{r}C_{1}\cdot 365 \cdot \dfrac{364.363 \dots (364-(r-2)+1)}{364^{r+2} }$
  3. $1- \dfrac{365 \cdot 364 \dots (365-r+1)}{365^{r}} - ^{r}C_{2} \cdot 365 \cdot \dfrac{ 364 \cdot 363 \dots (364-(r-2)+1)}{364^{r-2}}$
  4. $\dfrac{365 \cdot 364 \dots (365-r+1)}{365^{r}}$

review.answerKeySource: No official key is listed for 2008 in the historical paper/key index. Checked the original-paper listing and the reproduced GATE IT 2008 paper; the existing option C does not match the full general-r count.
review.independentCheck: The no-triple count is r!/365^r times the sum over j=0..floor(r/2) of C(365,j) C(365-j,r-2j)/2^j, counting every possible number j of double-occupied birthdays. Its complement gives the requested probability.
review.notes: HOLD: the original-paper sources confirm the displayed choices, and the historical key index lists no official 2008 key. Option C subtracts only the all-distinct and exactly-one-pair terms and has a malformed denominator; it omits cases with multiple pairs. Keep the existing answer record unchanged.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2008 | Question: 23
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following statements is true for every planar graph on $n$ vertices?

  1. The graph is connected
  2. The graph is Eulerian
  3. The graph has a vertex-cover of size at most $\frac{3n}{4}$
  4. The graph has an independent set of size at least $\frac{n}{3}$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Four-color theorem gives an independent class of size at least n/4; its complement is a vertex cover.

questions.title: GATE IT 2008 | Question: 24
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics

The exponent of $11$ in the prime factorization of $300!$ is

  1. $27$
  2. $28$

  4. $30$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2008 | Question: 24
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $P =\sum \limits_ {i\;\text{odd}}^{1\le i \le 2k} i$ and $Q = \sum\limits_{i\;\text{even}}^{1 \le i \le 2k} i$, where $k$ is a positive integer. Then

  1. $P = Q - k$
  2. $P = Q + k$
  3. $P = Q$
  4. $P = Q + 2k$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Closed-form odd and even sums give P=Q-k; key matches.

questions.title: GATE IT 2008 | Question: 25
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
In how many ways can $b$ blue balls and $r$ red balls be distributed in $n$ distinct boxes?

  1. $\frac{(n+b-1)!\,(n+r-1)!}{(n-1)!\,b!\,(n-1)!\,r!}$
  2. $\frac{(n+(b+r)-1)!}{(n-1)!\,(n-1)!\,(b+r)!}$
  3. $\frac{n!}{b!\,r!}$
  4. $\frac{(n + (b + r) - 1)!} {n!\,(b + r - 1)}$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Independent stars-and-bars counts for identical balls of each color multiply to option A.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2008 | Question: 25
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
A point on a curve is said to be an extremum if it is a local minimum or a local maximum. The number of distinct extrema for the curve $3x^4-16x^3+24x^2+37$ is

  1. $0$
  2. $1$
  3. $2$
  4. $3$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Derivative sign changes only at x=0; stationary x=2 is not an extremum.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2006 | Question: 18
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
We are given a set $X = \{X_1,\ldots,X_n\}$ where $X_i=2^i$.  A sample  $S\subseteq X$ is drawn by  selecting each $X_i$  independently with probability $P_i = \frac{1}{2}$ . The expected value of the smallest number in sample $S$ is:

  1. $\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)$
  2. $2$
  3. $\sqrt n$
  4. $n$

review.answerKeySource: No official key is listed for 2006 in the historical paper/key index. GateOverflow and the IIT Delhi solution give intended option D, but the stem leaves the empty sample undefined.
review.independentCheck: For each i, P(min(S)=2^i)=2^-i, so the weighted sum over nonempty outcomes is n. The empty sample has probability 2^-n; conditioning on nonempty gives n/(1-2^-n), while defining min(empty)=0 gives n.
review.notes: HOLD: the stem states neither a nonempty-sample condition nor min(empty)=0. The available historical key index lists no official 2006 key; option D is only the intended result under the unstated min(empty)=0 convention. Keep the existing answer record unchanged.

questions.title: GATE IT 2006 | Question: 21
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following first order logic formula in which $R$ is a binary relation symbol.

$∀x∀y (R(x, y) \implies R(y, x))$

The formula is

  1. satisfiable and valid
  2. satisfiable and so is its negation
  3. unsatisfiable but its negation is valid
  4. satisfiable but its negation is unsatisfiable

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Empty relation satisfies the formula; an asymmetric two-element relation satisfies its negation.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2006 | Question: 21
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
For each element in a set of size $2n$, an unbiased coin is tossed. The $2n$ coin tosses are independent. An element is chosen if the corresponding coin toss was a head. The probability that exactly $n$ elements are chosen is

  1. $\frac{^{2n}\mathrm{C}_n}{4^n}$
  2. $\frac{^{2n}\mathrm{C}_n}{2^n}$
  3. $\frac{1}{^{2n}\mathrm{C}_n}$
  4. $\frac{1}{2}$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Binomial probability is C(2n,n)/4^n; key matches.

questions.title: GATE IT 2006 | Question: 22
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
When a coin is tossed, the probability of getting a Head is $p, 0 < p < 1$. Let $N$ be the random variable denoting the number of tosses till the first Head appears, including the toss where the Head appears. Assuming that successive tosses are independent, the expected value of $N$ is

  1. $\dfrac{1}{p}$
  2. $\dfrac{1}{(1 - p)}$
  3. $\dfrac{1}{p^{2}}$
  4. $\dfrac{1}{(1 - p^{2})}$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Geometric waiting-time mean is 1/p; key matches.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2006 | Question: 22
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $E, F$ and $G$ be finite sets. Let

  • $X = (E ∩ F) - (F ∩ G)$ and
  • $Y = (E - (E ∩ G)) - (E - F)$.


Which one of the following is true?

  1. $X ⊂ Y$
  2. $X ⊃ Y$
  3. $X = Y$
  4. $X - Y ≠ \emptyset$ and $Y - X ≠ \emptyset$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Both set expressions simplify to E intersect F intersect G-complement.

questions.title: GATE IT 2006 | Question: 23
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $P$, $Q$ and $R$ be sets let Δ denote the symmetric difference operator defined as $PΔQ=(P \cup Q) - (P ∩ Q).$ Using Venn diagrams, determine which of the following is/are TRUE?

  1. $PΔ (Q ∩ R) = (P Δ Q) ∩ (P Δ R)$
  2. $P ∩ (Q ∩ R) =  (P ∩ Q) Δ (P Δ R)$
  1. I only
  2. II only
  3. Neither I nor II
  4. Both I and II

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Separate concrete counterexamples falsify both identities; neither is true.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2006 | Question: 23
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
$F$ is an $n\times n$ real matrix. $b$ is an $n\times 1$ real vector. Suppose there are two $n\times 1$ vectors, $u$ and $v$ such that, $u ≠ v$ and $Fu = b, Fv = b$. Which one of the following statements is false?

  1.    Determinant of $F$ is zero.  
  2.    There are an infinite number of solutions to $Fx = b$
  3.    There is an $x≠0$ such that $Fx = 0$
  4.    $F$ must have two identical rows

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Non-uniqueness implies singularity and nonzero kernel, but not duplicate rows.

questions.title: GATE IT 2006 | Question: 24
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
What is the cardinality of the set of integers $X$ defined below?

$X=\{n \mid 1 \leq n ≤ 123, n$ is not divisible by either $2$, $3$ or $5\}$

  1. $28$
  2. $33$
  3. $37$
  4. $44$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Inclusion-exclusion leaves 33 integers; key matches.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2006 | Question: 24
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Given a set of elements $N = {1, 2, ..., n}$ and two arbitrary subsets $A⊆N$ and $B⊆N$, how many of the n! permutations $\pi$ from $N$ to $N$ satisfy $\min(\pi(A)) = \min(\pi(B))$, where $\min(S)$ is the smallest integer in the set of integers $S$, and $\pi$(S) is the set of integers obtained by applying permutation $\pi$ to each element of $S$?

  1. $(n - |A ∪ B|) |A| |B|$
  2. $(|A|^{2} + |B|^{2})n^{2}$
  3. $n! \frac{|A ∩ B|}{|A ∪ B|}$
  4. $\dfrac{|A ∩ B|^2}{^n \mathrm{C}_{|A ∪ B|}}$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Uniform minimum over A union B gives overlap/union probability; nonempty-set precondition recorded.

questions.title: GATE IT 2006 | Question: 25
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the undirected graph $G$ defined as follows. The vertices of $G$ are bit strings of length $n$. We have an edge between vertex $u$ and vertex $v$ if and only if $u$ and $v$ differ in exactly one bit position (in other words, $v$ can be obtained from $u$ by flipping a single bit). The ratio of the chromatic number of $G$ to the diameter of $G$ is,

  1. $\frac{1}{\left(2^{n-1}\right)}$
  2. $\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)$
  3. $\left(\frac{2}{n}\right)$
  4. $\left(\frac{3}{n}\right)$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key, cross-checked against the GateOverflow discussion.
review.independentCheck: Re-derived from the question stem, then compared with the recorded answer key.
review.notes: Parity coloring gives chromatic number 2; opposite strings give diameter n.

HOLD.reason: The no-triple birthday probability must count all numbers of pairs; the listed option omits cases with multiple pairs and has a malformed denominator.
The random sample can be empty, where its minimum is undefined; the stem does not specify a convention or conditioning.
